question: In opioid overdose, naloxone reverses respiratory depression by competitively antagonising opioid receptors; repeated doses or an infusion may be needed because naloxone has a shorter half-life than most opioids.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is TRUE. Naloxone's short half-life (30–90 min) compared to most opioids means the patient can slip back into respiratory depression after the naloxone wears off — this is called re-narcotisation. An infusion running at two-thirds the effective reversal dose per hour is standard practice for long-acting opioids.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Naloxone is a pure opioid receptor antagonist with a half-life of only 30–90 minutes — far shorter than heroin (and especially methadone, which has a 24–36 hour half-life). Patients who respond to naloxone must be observed for re-narcotisation and may need a continuous IV infusion.
